title: Tool calling: schemas, validation, failure handling
story:
A tool call is a request from something that does not know your invariants and cannot be held to them. That sentence is the entire security and reliability posture, and everything below follows from taking it literally rather than as a caution.

Start with what the schema does and does not do. It describes the shape of a call — which arguments exist, what types they take — and, when the decoder is constrained, it guarantees that the call you receive has that shape. It guarantees nothing about whether the values make sense, whether the identifiers refer to anything real, whether the caller should be allowed to do this, or whether this is the third time the same action has been attempted in a minute. Those are your checks, at your boundary, written the way you would write them for a request arriving from the open internet. Not because the model is malicious, but because the model has no way to know your rules and no stake in them.

So validate: the types, the ranges, that referenced things exist, that the current user is permitted, that the arguments are consistent with each other. This is ordinary input validation and it is skipped constantly, because the call arrived from inside the system and looked well formed.

Now the part that is easy to miss, which is that your tool descriptions are part of the prompt. They are documentation read at runtime by the thing deciding which tool to use and what to pass it, and ambiguity in them comes back as wrong arguments. Name the units, because a field called duration will be given seconds by one caller and minutes by another, and the model is no different. Say what a call does when it fails. Say what the arguments mean when they interact. One clear example of correct use is worth several paragraphs of prose.

Design the surface, not only the functions. Fewer tools with clearly separated purposes produce better behaviour than many with overlapping ones, and this is where most tool-calling problems actually live. If two tools could plausibly apply to the same request, they will be chosen between badly, and the resulting mess looks like a reasoning failure when it is a naming failure. Before blaming the model for picking wrong, read your own two descriptions and ask whether a new colleague could reliably choose between them.

Treat errors as information rather than as an outcome. A returned error is read by the caller and used to decide what to do next, which means a message saying what was wrong and what would be valid can close the loop in one more turn, while a stack trace or a bare failure produces the same wrong call again. This is a small piece of writing that pays for itself immediately, and it is the rare case where a better error message is worth more than better logic.

Retries need the distinction you already know from every other distributed system. Some failures are worth repeating and some are not, so say which is which in what you return. Cap the attempts, because a loop that retries forever is a loop that fails forever. And never automatically retry an action with side effects unless the call carries something that makes a repeat harmless — a timeout and a success whose response was lost are indistinguishable from where the caller sits, so without that, retrying is guessing with somebody else's money.

The last one is the one to be firm about. Do not expose a tool whose worst-case invocation you would not authorise in advance, because sooner or later it will be invoked that way. The question to ask of each tool is not whether the model is reliable enough to be trusted with it. It is what happens when this is called with the worst arguments it accepts, and whether you can live with that happening without anyone present. If you cannot, the tool needs a narrower interface, a confirmation step, or a smaller blast radius — and that is a design change, not a prompt change.

problem.name: Accepting calls from a caller that does not know your rules
problem.shape: Something outside your control decides which action to invoke and with what arguments.
tell: arguments are used without validation because they arrived well formed
two available tools could plausibly serve the same request
errors are returned as stack traces or bare failures
a tool with side effects is retried automatically
a tool exists whose worst-case call nobody has thought about
problem.move: Validate every call at your boundary as you would an untrusted request, write tool descriptions as runtime documentation with units and failure behaviour, keep the tool surface small and non-overlapping, return errors that say what would be valid, and make side-effecting calls safe to repeat before allowing any retry.
problem.invariant: A schema constrains the shape of a call and says nothing about whether the values are permitted, consistent, or referring to anything real.
problem.breaks: A timeout and a success whose response was lost look identical to the caller, so retrying a side-effecting action without something that makes a repeat harmless is guessing.

cost.time: validation and a retry policy on every tool, which is the same tax as any external interface
cost.space: descriptions live in the window and are paid for on every request, so a large tool surface is expensive as well as confusing
cost.beats: trusting the call because it came from inside the system, which is how ordinary input validation gets skipped

worked.problem: How should a tool call be treated, and what decides whether a tool should exist at all?
worked.reasoning:
As a request from something that does not know my invariants and cannot be held to them. Not hostile — just uninformed about my rules and with no stake in them.

So the schema is doing less than it appears. It describes the shape of the call, and with a constrained decoder it guarantees that shape. It says nothing about whether the values make sense, whether the identifiers exist, whether this user may do this, or whether it is the third attempt in a minute. Those checks are mine, at my boundary, written as I would for a request from the open internet — and they get skipped constantly because the call came from inside the system and looked well formed.

I would also point out that tool descriptions are part of the prompt. They are documentation read at runtime by the thing choosing the tool and filling the arguments, so ambiguity there returns as wrong arguments. Name the units, because a field called duration gets seconds from one caller and minutes from another. Say what happens on failure. One clear example beats paragraphs.

Most tool-calling problems are actually surface design. Two tools that could plausibly serve the same request will be chosen between badly, and it looks like a reasoning failure when it is a naming failure — so before blaming the model, I read my own descriptions and ask whether a new colleague could choose reliably.

Errors are information, not an outcome. What I return is read and acted on, so a message saying what was wrong and what would be valid closes the loop in one turn, while a stack trace produces the same wrong call again.

Retries need the usual distributed-systems care: mark what is retryable, cap the attempts, and never auto-retry a side-effecting call unless a repeat is harmless, because a timeout and a lost success response are indistinguishable from the caller's side.

And what decides whether a tool should exist is its worst case, not the model's reliability. If I would not authorise the worst call the interface accepts, in advance and unattended, the tool needs a narrower interface, a confirmation step, or a smaller blast radius — which is a design change, not a prompt change.

problem.practice: Write down, for each tool you expose, the worst call its schema permits — the largest amount, the broadest selector, the most destructive combination that still type-checks. Read the list. The tools you would not sign off on unattended are the ones that need a narrower interface, and you will usually find at least one.

beats.broke: A well-formed call from inside the system gets trusted, but the caller does not know your invariants and has no stake in them.
beats.fix: Validate at your boundary like any untrusted request, write descriptions as runtime documentation, keep the surface small and separated, and return errors that say what would be valid.
beats.cost: Every tool carries validation, a retry policy and window space for its description, and the ones whose worst case is unacceptable need a design change rather than better instructions.

interview.q: How should a tool call be treated, and what decides whether a tool should exist at all?
interview.trap: Arguing about whether the model is reliable enough. The right question is the worst call the interface accepts and whether you would authorise it unattended — reliability does not change the blast radius.
interview.answer:
As a request from something that does not know my invariants and cannot be held to them. The schema constrains the shape and nothing else: not whether the values make sense, whether the identifiers exist, whether this user is permitted, or whether it is the third attempt in a minute. Those checks are mine, at my boundary, written as for a request from the open internet — and they get skipped precisely because the call came from inside the system and looked well formed.

I would also treat the tool descriptions as part of the prompt, since they are documentation read at runtime: name the units, say what failure does, give one example. And most tool-calling problems are surface design — two tools that could plausibly serve the same request will be chosen between badly, which looks like a reasoning failure and is a naming failure.

Errors are information. A message saying what was wrong and what would be valid closes the loop in one turn; a stack trace produces the same wrong call again. Retries need the usual care: mark retryable versus terminal, cap attempts, and never auto-retry a side-effecting call unless a repeat is harmless, because a timeout and a lost success response look identical from the caller's side.

What decides whether a tool should exist is its worst case. If I would not authorise the worst call its schema permits, unattended and in advance, then it needs a narrower interface, a confirmation step or a smaller blast radius — a design change, not a prompt change.
